Germany maintained credible NATO nuclear-sharing arrangements and selected the F-35 aircraft for that role, while remaining non-nuclear and not controlling the weapons (E005, E010, E011). This was a risk-bearing choice that preserved deterrence but drew independent criticism as adverse to arms control (E012). On the favorable side, Germany supported nuclear verification, funded biological-weapons investigation readiness and reference laboratories, and participated in multilateral biological-threat mitigation and simulation work (E006, E007, E008). These actions show institutional investment in safeguards and expertise, although they are not uniquely attributable to Scholz and do not prove effectiveness.
